newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Fired woman doctor ignites sex discrimination dispute.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Fired woman doctor ignites sex discrimination dispute.

text.p: Carol Bender admits to a certain assertiveness on the job but says that made her no different from many of the male doctors at Suburban Hospital -- until she was shown the door.
"My style is laid back until someone is sick," she said. "Then I have the intensity that is required."

Sometimes she swore while working at the hospital, or asked why her patients received what she considered poor treatment. Last February, after about 20 years of treating patients at Suburban, Bender received a termination notice. The 392-bed hospital is in Bethesda, Maryland, just outside Washington.

The Maryland Commission on Human Relations has charged Suburban Hospital with unlawful sex discrimination and retaliation against Bender for pursuing her rights under the law. The commission, Maryland's counterpart to the federal Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, enforces the state's law against discrimination.

"We investigated to find out whether she was being treated differently than male doctors that exhibit the same kind of behaviour. She was," Lee Hoshall, assistant general counsel at the commission, said.

The hospital says it is confident its actions will be upheld in court because it considers what happened was discipline, not discrimination. "The hospital does not believe this is a case of discrimination in any way. The hospital believes this is a case involving a long-standing pattern of disruptive behaviour which could compromise patient care," spokeswoman Cynthia Merz said.

Merz was reluctant to discuss details of the case, but Bender and her attorney provided her side of the story. Bender said the hospital apparently began keeping a file on her behaviour in the 1980s and that the doctors spearheading the campaign against her were male, although there were also complaints from female staff.

"Whatever they had to put up with from the male doctors, they felt they could have a different standard for women. The same qualities that were considered strengths in men were considered problems in women," Bender said. "I do not fit the role. (They think) you should be subservient, deferential, pleasing. But if my patients were sicker than someone else's, I went forward."

Once when she asked to see an old chart on a patient, for example, staffers complained that she was demanding, she said. "If a man did that sort of thing, they'd say, 'Isn't this a wonderful doctor. Boy! Does he want to be on top of things!'"

Bender acknowledged some incidents involved cursing. "In private conversations, I used the 'f-word' two times." Once it happened when one of her patients with coronary disease was admitted to the hospital and given stomach antacids instead of the appropriate care, Bender said. The other time was after she learned that a young woman who came to the emergency room with strep throat had been given many unnecessary tests.

Bender's lawyer, John Singleton, said most of the complaints about his client dated to before 1988 and she had modified her behaviour since then. "One mellows. You just do over time, you are not as brash and want to achieve everything in five seconds."

But Bender's relations with the hospital did not improve. In 1992, when a hospital panel recommended she have counselling in order to keep treating patients at Suburban, Bender went to the state commission and it began investigating her case.

By last year, Singleton said, Suburban was willing to drop the counselling request if Bender would drop her complaint with the commission. "But they said she had to drop it and say they didn't do anything wrong. She won't do that," he said.

Bender's case will be heard on March 3 by a state administrative law judge. If the judge agrees with the human relations commission, Bender could be reinstated and get back pay for the business she says she has lost as some patients left her for doctors who are linked to Suburban.
Either side could appeal to circuit court in Maryland, or Bender could turn to the federal courts.

Hoshall said the case was significant because as a private physician Bender was not directly employed by the hospital. But the law should still apply, he said. "Without a hospital, she can't really practice medicine."
